{{Short description|Method in algebraic topology}}
{{No footnotes|date=September 2010}}

In [[algebraic topology]] the '''cap product''' is a method of adjoining a [[chain (algebraic topology)|chain]] of degree <math>p</math> with a [[cochain]] of degree <math>q</math>, such that <math>q\leq p</math>, to form a composite chain of degree <math>p-q</math>.   It was introduced by [[Eduard Čech]] in 1936, and independently by [[Hassler Whitney]] in 1938.

==Definition==
Let ''X'' be a [[topological space]] and ''R'' a coefficient ring. The cap product is a [[bilinear map]] on [[singular homology]] and [[cohomology]]
:<math>\frown\;: H_p(X;R)\times H^q(X;R) \rightarrow H_{p-q}(X;R).</math>

defined by contracting a [[singular chain]] <math>\sigma : \Delta^p \rightarrow X</math> with a singular [[cochain]] <math> \psi \in C^q(X;R), </math> by the formula:

:<math> \sigma \frown \psi = \psi(\sigma|_{[v_0, \ldots, v_q]}) \sigma|_{[v_q, \ldots, v_p]}.</math>

Here, the notation <math>\sigma|_{[v_0, \ldots, v_q]}</math> indicates the restriction of the [[simplicial map]] <math>\sigma</math> to its face spanned by the vectors of the base.

==Interpretation==
In analogy with the interpretation of the [[cup product]] in terms of the [[Künneth formula]], we can explain the existence of the cap product in the following way. Using [[Cellular approximation theorem#CW approximation|CW approximation]] we may assume that <math>X</math> is a [[CW complex|CW-complex]] and <math>C_\bullet(X)</math> (and <math>C^\bullet(X)</math>) is the complex of its cellular chains (or cochains, respectively). Consider then the composition  
<math display="block"> C_\bullet(X) \otimes C^\bullet(X) \overset{\Delta_* \otimes \mathrm{Id}}{\longrightarrow} C_\bullet(X) \otimes C_\bullet(X) \otimes C^\bullet(X) \overset{\mathrm{Id} \otimes \varepsilon}{\longrightarrow} C_\bullet(X) </math>
where we are taking [[Künneth theorem|tensor products of chain complexes]], <math> \Delta \colon X \to X \times X</math> is the [[diagonal functor|diagonal map]] which induces the map
<math display="block">\Delta_* \colon C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet(X \times X)\cong C_\bullet(X)\otimes C_\bullet(X)</math>
on the chain complex, and <math>\varepsilon \colon C_p(X) \otimes C^q(X) \to \mathbb{Z}</math> is the [[evaluation map (topology)|evaluation map]] (always 0 except for <math>p=q</math>).

This composition then passes to the quotient to define the cap product <math> \frown \colon H_\bullet(X) \times H^\bullet(X) \to H_\bullet(X)</math>, and looking carefully at the above composition shows that it indeed takes the form of maps <math> \frown \colon H_p(X) \times H^q(X) \to H_{p-q}(X)</math>, which is always zero for <math>p < q</math>.

==Fundamental class==

For any point <math>x</math> in <math>M</math>, we have the long-exact sequence in homology (with coefficients in <math>R</math>) of the pair <math>(M, M - x)</math> (See [[Relative homology]]) 

:<math>\cdots \to H_n(M - {x}; R) \stackrel{i_*}{\to} H_n(M; R) \stackrel{j_*}{\to} H_n (M, M - {x}; R) \stackrel{\partial}{\to} H_{n-1}(M - {x}; R)  \to \cdots .</math>

An element <math>[M]</math> of <math>H_n(M; R)</math> is called the [[fundamental class]] for <math>M</math> if <math>j_*([M])</math> is a generator of <math>H_n (M, M - {x}; R)</math>. A fundamental class of <math>M</math> exists if <math>M</math> is closed and [[orientability|R-orientable]]. In fact, if <math>M</math> is a closed, connected and <math>R</math>-orientable manifold, the map <math>H_n(M; R) \stackrel{j_*}{\to} H_n (M, M - {x}; R)</math> is an isomorphism for all <math>x</math> in <math>R</math> and hence, we can choose any generator of <math>H_n(M; R)</math> as the fundamental class.

==Relation with Poincaré duality==

For a closed <math>R</math>-orientable n-manifold <math>M</math> with fundamental class <math>[M]</math> in <math>H_n(M; R)</math> (which we can choose to be any generator of <math>H_n(M; R)</math>), the cap product map <math display="block"> H^k(M; R)\to H_{n-k}(M; R), 
\alpha\mapsto [M]\frown \alpha </math>
is an isomorphism for all <math>k</math>. This result is famously called [[Poincaré duality]].

==The slant product==

If in the above discussion one replaces <math>X\times X</math> by <math>X\times Y</math>, the construction can be (partially) replicated starting from the mappings
<math display="block"> C_\bullet(X\times Y) \otimes C^\bullet(Y)\cong C_\bullet(X) \otimes C_\bullet(Y) \otimes C^\bullet(Y) \overset{\mathrm{Id} \otimes \varepsilon}{\longrightarrow} C_\bullet(X) </math>
and
<math display="block"> C^\bullet(X\times Y) \otimes C_\bullet(Y)\cong C^\bullet(X) \otimes C^\bullet(Y) \otimes C_\bullet(Y) \overset{\mathrm{Id} \otimes \varepsilon}{\longrightarrow} C^\bullet(X) </math>

to get, respectively, '''slant products''' <math>/ </math>:
<math display="block"> H_p(X\times Y;R) \otimes H^q(Y;R) \rightarrow H_{p-q}(X;R)</math> and
<math display="block"> H^p(X\times Y;R) \otimes H_q(Y;R) \rightarrow H^{p-q}(X;R).</math>

In case <math>X=Y</math>, the first one is related to the cap product by the diagonal map: <math> \Delta_*(a)/\phi = a\frown \phi</math>. 

These ‘products’ are in some ways more like division than multiplication, which is reflected in their notation.

==Equations==
The boundary of a cap product is given by :

:<math>\partial(\sigma \frown \psi) = (-1)^q(\partial \sigma \frown \psi - \sigma \frown \delta \psi). </math>

Given a map ''f'' the induced maps satisfy :

:<math> f_*( \sigma ) \frown \psi = f_*(\sigma \frown f^* (\psi)). </math>

The cap and [[cup product]] are related by :

:<math> \psi(\sigma \frown \varphi) = (\varphi \smile \psi)(\sigma)</math>

where

:<math>\sigma : \Delta ^{p+q} \rightarrow X</math>,  <math> \psi \in C^q(X;R)</math> and <math> \varphi \in C^p(X;R). </math>

If <math>\sigma</math> is allowed to be of higher degree than <math>p+q</math>, the last identity takes a more general form

:<math>  (\sigma \frown \varphi) \frown \psi = \sigma \frown (\varphi \smile \psi) </math>

which makes <math>H_{\ast}(X;R)</math> into a right <math>H^{\ast}(X;R)</math>-[[module (mathematics)|module]].
